CODING AGENT · DOCUMENTATION REVIEW

OpenCode: models, permissions and safety

OpenCode supports multiple model providers. Check your version before configuring permissions, then verify the individual tool result when running headless.

English edition published October 26, 2026. This adapts our Chinese project review; migration and security sources were rechecked on that date.

Evidence boundary: This is a documentation-based review, not a hands-on test of coding performance. We inspected the configured rule order and ran four non-interactive file-write checks with a local fixture. The Chinese edition's original October 15 editorial score has not been revalidated for V2. We do not turn GitHub stars into a quality or search-demand claim.

OpenCode permissions: match the installed version

Run opencode --version first. For V2, ask before edits, shell commands and access outside the project with the rules below. Keep a copy of existing configuration before merging; managed and agent rules can change the effective result.

Which OpenCode version are you using?

V2 rulesV1 syntaxCheck version

V2: ask for edits, commands and outside-project access

{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "permissions": [
    {
      "action": "edit",
      "resource": "*",
      "effect": "ask"
    },
    {
      "action": "shell",
      "resource": "*",
      "effect": "ask"
    },
    {
      "action": "external_directory",
      "resource": "*",
      "effect": "ask"
    }
  ]
}

The last matching rule wins. Merge these entries into your existing permissions array, then check later overrides. This controls approval prompts; it does not isolate shell processes, files or network access.

  1. In a disposable project without secrets, request one small file edit. Confirm a prompt appears.
  2. Reject once and inspect the file; then test one harmless shell command and a read outside that project separately.
  3. If a prompt is missing, inspect configuration priority and the active agent before granting more access. A successful edit alone does not verify the other permission actions.

V1: keep version-specific syntax

The following is the V1 example recorded in our October 29 documentation review. Do not paste the native V2 array into V1:

{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "permission": "ask"
}

V2 intends to retain supported V1 configuration, so converting every working file is optional. Use the migration guide to check your complete configuration instead of mixing individual fields.

Version unknown or prompts missing

Record the output of opencode --version and your installation method. The current installation guide describes V2. Check the configuration priority, including managed settings and agent rules; avoid an automatic approval mode while checking whether a request asks.

Permission examples were reviewed on November 23, 2026. The rule-order check below was run separately on November 28.

Why OpenCode V2 did not ask before an edit

  1. Check the active agent and workspace. In that project, run opencode debug agents --standalone and read the active agent’s permissions array. Keep the raw output local because it can include configuration details.
  2. Find every rule matching the action and resource. An edit rule applies to edit, write and patch operations. A later specific deny blocks the edit. A later matching allow explains why the client may proceed without asking. Check agent rules, saved approvals and administrator policies before changing anything.
  3. Use a new disposable project and a harmless file to verify whether the client asks, blocks or proceeds. For a shell command or a path outside the project, test that action separately.

In OpenCode V2.4.1, we inspected the built-in Build agent in two empty projects. Both contained edit * → ask and edit notes.txt → deny. The CLI reported each rule in the order configured. Under the documented last-match rule, putting the specific rule last yields deny for notes.txt. Reversing the order yields ask at the configured-rule stage. The configuration inspection shows the order. The separate runtime check shows what happened to the file.

Download the two configurations and reported rule orders. Reproduce on macOS with the inspection script and loopback-only policy. Pass the path to the V2 binary followed by the policy file. Official permission rules checked November 28, 2026.

How to verify a blocked write in OpenCode run

When opencode run is non-interactive, an ask rule can leave the file untouched without displaying a prompt. Run a harmless edit in a disposable project with --format json, then check the tool_use event’s part.state and read the file. A successful process exit alone cannot confirm that the write happened.

OpenCode 2.4.1, Build agent, writing notes.txt
Final ruleWrite resultFile
denyPermission deniedSame
askRejected without promptingSame
allowTool completedEdited

All three runs exited 0 after the synthetic model returned its final reply. A fourth run with auto-approval enabled still blocked the configured deny. For scripts, require both a completed event for the intended tool and the expected file change.

Download the four runtime checks. We used a local model fixture in isolated macOS test projects. This covers the write tool and the non-interactive CLI. Interactive approval dialogs, shell commands and paths outside the project were outside the test. See the official approval behavior.

What should you evaluate?

Our existing project review focuses on OpenCode's provider choice and coding workflow: reading a repository, making changes and invoking tools. Provider flexibility is useful only if the models you intend to use work with your actual tasks and budget.

Do not interpret the software's license as a promise of free model usage. Check the terms and pricing of the provider you connect, decide which repository data may leave the machine, and record those choices before a trial. This page does not provide a current price comparison.

Before installation: distinguish OpenCode 1 from 2

The official migration guide says both generations use the same command name and are not installed side by side by default. An installation can replace the earlier binary. Identify the existing installation and follow the matching official instructions rather than mixing tutorials.

  • Keep a readable copy of your working configuration before migrating.
  • Review plugins, server integrations and terminal configuration: these have breaking changes.
  • Validate models, credentials, permissions and MCP connections after migration.
  • Do not point V1 at configuration converted to V2-only formats.

These are migration checks, not a claim that we performed the migration on your operating system. The upstream guide is the authority for version-specific details.

Approval prompts are not a sandbox

The project's published security model states that the agent is not sandboxed. Approval prompts do not provide process, filesystem or network isolation. For isolation, the project recommends a container or virtual machine.

  • Server mode: when enabling it, configure authentication and restrict network exposure. The security document identifies OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD as the password setting.
  • Model providers: their own policies govern data sent to them.
  • External MCP servers: assess their behavior and data handling separately; they are outside the project's core trust boundary.

Our practical recommendation: use a disposable repository without secrets for a first trial. A container with broad host mounts is not automatically an adequate boundary; review what access you actually grant.

A small trial you can reproduce

The following is our proposed evaluation procedure, not a report of completed testing. Keep the same task and acceptance criteria when comparing runs.

  1. Write down the setup. Record the installed version, operating system, chosen model, provider and permission configuration. Never publish API keys.
  2. Choose a bounded change. Use a disposable copy of a small repository with a known passing test command. Save its initial revision and test result.
  3. Ask for an explanation first. Check whether the agent identifies the relevant files and constraints before permitting edits.
  4. Allow one change. Review the proposed commands and resulting diff. Record unexpected file changes and approval requests.
  5. Run the same tests. Keep the actual output, including failures. A confident answer is not evidence that the task works.
  6. Check recovery and cost. Confirm you can restore the disposable copy, inspect provider usage, then decide whether to expand access.

A useful result contains the task, before-and-after diff, test output, failures and measured cost. Until those artifacts exist, treat claims about speed, reliability and value as unverified.
